newsitem.title: USA: Learning About mice, hippies, and anywhere machines.
newsitem.headline: Learning About mice, hippies, and anywhere machines.

text.p: Is your child "rodent-ready?"

If you've watched kids zip through video games like they were born with a mouse in one hand, it may be hard to believe that some preschoolers -- and plenty of older children as well -- have no mouse-hand-eye coordination.

They think you move a mouse by picking it up. Their ability to get the cursor to a spot on the screen is as klutzy as a baby's first steps. Clicking the mouse button while holding the mouse still is a major challenge.

That's the beauty of "Reader Rabbit Toddler" for ages 18 months to 3 years (Windows/Macintosh, $30, 800-227-5609, http://www.learningco.com). "Toddler" offers a series of games that are gloriously forgiving of a child who has no mouse manipulation skills.

If the player moves the cursor near an object the youngster wants, the game automatically "grabs" and holds onto it until the cursor approaches the spot where the child wants it to go. Then the grip is released and the object snaps into place.
I tried it with Alex, a 3-year-old with virtually no mouse skills. In just an hour, you could see his mouse-hand-eye coordination improve dramatically.

Even if a child doesn't need to master the mouse, "Toddler" is a fine CD-ROM in its own right. The "Rainbow Rock" game colours pictures by swiping a crayon over the picture. "Follow Me Theatre" has eight popular songs, complete with hand motions. In "Sky Shapers," the player pops a shape into a hole to create pictures. "Bubble Castle" is an arcade game where the mouse is used to pop bubbles.
Obviously, children can learn basic mouse skills on their own. But "Reader Rabbit Toddler" is a great way to get them started.
It's available through mid-August for just $10 if you buy a package with a mail-in rebate.
Attention ex-hippies or other children of the '60s. It has now been officially determined that you lived in an "exotic period" in world history.
That's the word from an IBM news release for "Crayola Magic Wardrobe," a children's CD-ROM that makes computer-generated paper dolls.

The game also lets you "travel through time and visit 12 exotic periods," including Ancient Egypt, Imperial China, Elizabethan England, the American West and -- drumroll, please -- the Age of the American Hippie.

Perhaps it shouldn't be surprising that the decade of psychedelic fashions, eight-track tapes, free love, communes, clogs and copper bracelets to ward off disease would rank alongside Ancient Egypt on the exotic scale. After all, except for the music of the era, most of the trappings of the American Hippie period are now alien (or just plain silly) to a generation whose legacy has evolved into business suits, condoms and corporate greed.

"Magic Wardrobe" (Windows/Macintosh, $30, ages 6 to 12) tries to give kids insights into the various periods using three- or four-page diary entries from each era, along with a brief story about a notable woman of the time. In the Mediaeval era, the woman is Eleanor of Aquitaine, who became queen of both England and France. In the '60s, it's folk singer Joan Baez.

But sometimes it's the clothes themselves that give the best perspective on the trappings and foibles of various eras. "Magic Wardrobe" offers youngsters information about the clothes, if they are not too busy playing with the paper dolls. And if your children or grandchildren want to snicker about
what people wore in that "exotic" Hippie Era, take some comfort in the fact that in 20 or 30 years, today's kids are going to have to explain tongue rings to their offspring.
Nobody says a computer game has to be a sophisticated multimedia experience to be entertaining.

"Uncle Julius and the Anywhere Machine" from AHA! Software (Windows) is quaintly retro compared with the typical game you can pick up for $40 or $50 at a computer store. You can't move through a virtual reality world. There's no sophisticated animation. The music and sound effects are pretty rudimentary.
But the puzzles in this tale of an inventor who builds a teleportation machine are strangely captivating.

In the story, Uncle Julius has zapped himself into a world where the people believe that you can't have too many laws. After Uncle Julius gets arrested on suspicion of acting suspiciously, players must use his machine to visit various sites in a quest to earn enough ducats to buy the cane that will teleport him safely home.
The game is hard to pigeonhole. At first glance, it looks like it was designed for elementary school children. But some of the topics seem to make it designed for teens and grownups.
My chief complaint after playing the first half is the hint system is much too rudimentary. It's almost no help in some of the places where you find yourself wondering what to do next.

"Uncle Julius" is shareware, which means you can download it for free by visiting the game's Internet home page (http://www.familygames.com/anywhere.html). About one-fourth of the way through, you are asked to pay $19 so you can get the registration code that unlocks the rest of the game. The shareware system gives you the chance to try it before you buy it.
If you're not looking for anything flashy, "Uncle Julius" is worth sampling.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
